title: Everything in fives: the outer world and the body
theme: Three groups of five outside and three groups of five within are set side by side, and a seer’s saying concludes that the whole is fivefold and that the inner fives complete the outer.

words.meaning: the self (here, the body of the whole)
with regard to beings, the outer
with regard to the self, the inner

words.context: Kūranārāyaṇa: «रसग्रहणहेतुः वाक्» — he takes it as the tongue, organ of taste

sandhi.rule: ī before a dissimilar vowel becomes y: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
A visarga after au becomes r before the voiced d. diśaḥ before a becomes diśo, and the a is elided (avagraha): P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel; aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: Before a vowel other than a, aḥ loses its visarga and the hiatus stays (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)); before the voiced v, oṣadhayaḥ becomes oṣadhayo (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)).
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः). a + a → ā: P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः). The base prints māṃsaṃ and snāvāsthi without a space.

sandhi_exceptions.note: अधिविधाय ऋषिः: ā before ṛ is left unjoined, as P. 6.1.128 (ऋत्यकः) allows (a vowel of the ak group before ṛ may stand unchanged). Ordinary sandhi would give adhividhāyarṣiḥ; every witness has the hiatus.

samasa.meaning: the intermediate quarters (north-east and the rest)
with regard to beings (the outer world)
with regard to the self (the body)

morphology.note: Nominative singular of div/dyu, ‘sky’, with vṛddhi in the strong stem (dyau-).

A secondary derivative of paṅkti, the metre of five pādas (and ‘a row of five’), with vṛddhi of the first syllable: ‘belonging to the paṅkti, fivefold’. Śaṅkara connects it with the sacrifice, which the Veda calls pāṅkta: «पञ्चपदा पङ्क्तिः पाङ्क्तो यज्ञः».
Reduplicated (thematic) aorist of vac, ‘to speak’: ‘he said’.
Present of spṛ (fifth class, -ṇo-), ‘to fill, to strengthen, to sustain’. Śaṅkara glosses ‘strengthens, fills, is known as one with’ («एकात्मतयोपलभ्यत इत्येतत्»).
Nominative singular of the neuter n-stem snāvan, ‘sinew’.
Nominative singular of majjan, ‘marrow’ (an n-stem; nominative majjā).

translation.literal: Earth, mid-region, sky, the quarters, the intermediate quarters; fire, wind, sun, moon, stars; waters, plants, trees, space, the self (body): thus [the series] with regard to beings. Now with regard to the self: out-breath, diffused breath, in-breath, up-breath, middle breath; eye, ear, mind, speech, skin; hide, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow. Having set this out, the seer said: ‘Fivefold indeed is this all. By the fivefold, indeed, one fills the fivefold.’
translation.readable: Earth, the space between, the sky, the four quarters and the quarters between them; fire, wind, sun, moon and stars; water, plants, trees, space and the body of the whole — that is the outer world. Now the inner: the five breaths; eye, ear, mind, speech and touch; skin, flesh, sinew, bone and marrow. Having arranged all this, the seer said: ‘All this is in fives. With the fives within, one fills out the fives without.’

syntax: Six lists of five nouns in the nominative, without verbs: three ‘with regard to beings’ (adhibhūtam) and, after atha, three ‘with regard to the self’ (adhyātmam). An absolutive (adhividhāya, ‘having set out’) introduces the seer’s saying with avocat, ‘said’; the saying is two sentences closed by iti — a nominal sentence (pāṅktaṃ vā idaṃ sarvam) and a verbal one whose subject is unexpressed (‘one fills’).

ambiguities.topic: What is ‘ātman’ at the end of the outer series?
ambiguities.note: In a list of beings — waters, plants, trees, space — ātman is unexpected. Śaṅkara takes it as Virāj, the cosmic body, ‘because beings are the subject’ («आत्मेति विराट् , भूताधिकारात्»); Gopālānanda similarly. Madhva reads it as the principle of I-making: «आत्मा अहङ्कारतत्त्वम्».
Śaṅkara allows two readings: the Veda itself, or some seer who had this vision — «ऋषिः वेदः एतद्दर्शनसम्पन्नो वा कश्चिदृषिः». The text names no one.

The subject of spṛṇoti is not expressed. Śaṅkara: the inner fives, by sameness of number, fill out the outer, so that the two are known as one; the knower becomes Prajāpati. Kūranārāyaṇa and Gopālānanda take spṛṇoti as ‘protects, sustains’ («स्पृणोति - व्याप्नोति, पालयति»; «स्पृणोति पालयति»), the result being the power to sustain the world.

ambiguities.topic: Why only three outer groups are ‘adhibhūta’
ambiguities.note: Strictly only the third group (waters … ātman) consists of beings. Śaṅkara explains the word as standing for all three outer groups: «इत्यधिभूतमिति अधिलोकाधिदैवतपाङ्क्तद्वयोपलक्षणार्थम्».

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose: six lists of five, and a two-sentence saying.

beginner: This passage is a list, and the list has a pattern. First it names fifteen things in the world outside us, in three groups of five: earth, air-space, sky and the directions; fire, wind, sun, moon and stars; water, plants, trees, space and the whole body of the world. Then it names fifteen things inside the body, again in three groups of five: five kinds of breath; eye, ear, mind, speech and touch; skin, flesh, sinew, bone and marrow. A seer then sums it up: everything comes in fives, and the fives inside us match and complete the fives outside. The commentators say the point is a meditation: to see the world and one’s own body as built on the same plan, and so as not truly separate.
analogy: Like two halves of a torn ticket: each half is incomplete, but the edges match exactly, and fitting them together shows that they were always one piece.

commentary.q: What does the passage actually say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It lists three groups of five ‘with regard to beings’ — worlds and quarters; fire, wind, sun, moon, stars; waters, plants, trees, space, self — and three ‘with regard to the self’ — five breaths; eye, ear, mind, speech, skin; hide, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow. It says that a seer, having set this out, declared that all this is fivefold, and that by the fivefold one fills the fivefold. It does not say what is to be done with this; the commentators call it a meditation.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara connects the number with the paṅkti metre of five pādas and with the sacrifice, which the Veda calls pāṅkta: «पाङ्क्तश्च यज्ञः», «पञ्चपदा पङ्क्तिः पाङ्क्तो यज्ञः». To see the whole as fivefold is therefore to see it as a sacrifice; by that sacrifice, imagined, one reaches Prajāpati, whose nature is fivefold: «तेन यज्ञेन परिकल्पितेन पाङ्क्तात्मकं प्रजापतिमभिसम्पद्यते».

commentary.q: How are the six groups named?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara names each group: the five of worlds, of deities and of beings («लोकपाङ्क्तम्», «देवतापाङ्क्तम्», «भूतपाङ्क्तम्») outside; the five of breath, of the senses and of the bodily tissues («वायुपाङ्क्तम्», «इन्द्रियपाङ्क्तम्», «धातुपाङ्क्तम्») within. The two halves, he says, are all there is: «एतावद्धीदं सर्वमध्यात्मं बाह्यं च पाङ्क्तमेव».

commentary.q: What is the fruit of the meditation?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: For Śaṅkara, one who knows ‘all this is fivefold’ becomes one with Prajāpati: «एवं पाङ्क्तमिदं सर्वमिति यो वेद, स प्रजापत्यात्मैव भवतीत्यर्थः». The modern commentator Gopālānanda reads spṛṇoti as ‘protects’ and the fruit as sovereignty: «पाङ्केन - पाङ्कदृष्ट्योपास्यमानेनानेन पाङ्कं पृथिव्यादि स्पृणोति पालयति, साम्राज्यं लभते इति भावः» (his printed text spells pāṅkta as पाङ्क).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Ordinary sandhi would fuse ā and ṛ into ar (adhividhāyarṣiḥ). The recited text keeps the two vowels apart, as Pāṇini allows before ṛ: P. 6.1.128 (ऋत्यकः). Every witness of this edition has the hiatus. The variant avāntaradiśāḥ (long ā), read by the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text, is a by-form of the same word.

advaita.text: The meditation continues the meditation on Brahman as the four calls, now in the form of the fivefold: «तस्यैवेदानीं पृथिव्यादिपाङ्क्तस्वरूपेणोपासनमुच्यते». It is an upāsana of Brahman with qualities whose fruit is identity with Prajāpati; Śaṅkara does not present it as the knowledge of the unconditioned.

visistadvaita.text: Kūranārāyaṇa calls the passage a particular meditation taught as a limb of knowledge: «इदानीं ध्यानविशेषं ज्ञानाङ्गत्वेनोपदिशति». The seer is the Veda («ऋषिर्वेदात्मा»), and by the fives held together in meditation one pervades and protects the universe: «पाङ्कं - विश्वं स्पृणोति - व्याप्नोति, पालयति» (his printed text spells pāṅkta as पाङ्क).

dvaita.text: Madhva cites a verse he attributes to the Tattvasaṃhitā («इति तत्त्वसंहितायाम्»): it is Hari himself, in the form of Nārāyaṇa and his other forms, who strengthens the six fives by the fivefold — «पृथिव्याद्यं पाङ्क्तषट्कं पाङ्क्तेनैव स्वयं हरिः». The seer who spoke is Viṣṇu. This is a verse cited by Madhva; this edition cannot verify it as a quotation of an independent work.

schools.disagreement: All read a meditation on correspondences. They differ on its fruit (identity with Prajāpati for Śaṅkara; the power to sustain the world for Kūranārāyaṇa and Gopālānanda) and on who does the ‘filling’ (the meditator for Śaṅkara and Kūranārāyaṇa; Hari himself for Madhva).

parallels.quote: स एष पाङ्क्तो यज्ञः पाङ्क्तः पशुः पाङ्क्तः पुरुषः पाङ्क्तमिदं सर्वं
parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka also declares the sacrifice, the animal, the person and ‘all this’ to be pāṅkta, fivefold.

contemporary.text: We often picture ourselves as a self set against a world. This passage lays the two side by side and finds the same structure in each: the breath within answers the wind without, the eye answers the sun, the body answers the earth. It does not deny that there is an inside and an outside; it says they match. A self-image built on that correspondence is harder to inflate and harder to isolate. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Can you name something outside you that your body depends on every minute?
reflect.deeper: Why might the Upaniṣad teach a correspondence between body and world before it teaches the knowledge of Brahman?
reflect.practice: Take one breath and notice the air coming from outside and going back out. For that breath, try not to draw a line between the two.

references.text: In the six-commentary edition, Kūranārāyaṇa’s comment on this anuvāka is followed by a second comment marked ‘आ.भा.’; it is not identified in this edition’s sources, and nothing in it is quoted here.

flags.note: The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text read avāntaradiśāḥ for the base’s avāntaradiśaḥ (corrections.json); both are forms of ‘intermediate quarters’.
The digital text of Kūranārāyaṇa and Gopālānanda (OCR-derived) spells pāṅkta as पाङ्क throughout; quotations keep the printed spelling.
